```{r setup}
suppressPackageStartupMessages({ library(haven); library(fixest) })
f1 <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f", x)
f2 <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)
f3 <- function(x) sprintf("%.3f", x)
# Baker simulation (Cunningham, Remix ch. 10): 1,000 firms, 1980-2009, four cohorts of 250 treated in 1986/92/98/2004.
b <- as.data.frame(read_dta("data/baker.dta"))
b <- b[, c("id", "group", "year", "treat_date", "treat", "y", "y2", "time_til")]
# Cheng and Hoekstra (2013), all 50 states this time: cohorts 2005-2009 and 29 never-treated.
cst <- as.data.frame(read_dta("data/castle.dta"))
cst$post <- as.numeric(!is.na(cst$effyear) & cst$year >= cst$effyear)

# Goodman-Bacon (2021) decomposition, by hand, for a balanced panel with absorbing treatment.
bacon <- function(d, yvar, idvar = "id", tvar = "year", gvar = "treat_date") {
  Tn <- length(unique(d[[tvar]])); t0 <- min(d[[tvar]]); tmax <- max(d[[tvar]]); N <- length(unique(d[[idvar]]))
  d$D <- as.numeric(!is.na(d[[gvar]]) & d[[tvar]] >= d[[gvar]])
  Dt <- d$D - ave(d$D, d[[idvar]]) - ave(d$D, d[[tvar]]) + mean(d$D); VD <- mean(Dt^2)
  units <- d[!duplicated(d[[idvar]]), c(idvar, gvar)]
  grps <- sort(unique(units[[gvar]][!is.na(units[[gvar]])])); grps <- grps[grps > t0]
  nU <- mean(is.na(units[[gvar]])); nk <- sapply(grps, function(g) sum(units[[gvar]] == g, na.rm = TRUE) / N)
  Dbar <- (tmax - grps + 1) / Tn
  m <- function(gsel, yr) mean(d[[yvar]][gsel & d[[tvar]] >= yr[1] & d[[tvar]] <= yr[2]])
  out <- list()
  for (i in seq_along(grps)) {
    k <- grps[i]; gk <- !is.na(d[[gvar]]) & d[[gvar]] == k
    if (nU > 0) {
      gU <- is.na(d[[gvar]]); nkU <- nk[i] / (nk[i] + nU)
      dd <- (m(gk, c(k, tmax)) - m(gk, c(t0, k - 1))) - (m(gU, c(k, tmax)) - m(gU, c(t0, k - 1)))
      w <- (nk[i] + nU)^2 * nkU * (1 - nkU) * Dbar[i] * (1 - Dbar[i]) / VD
      out[[length(out) + 1]] <- data.frame(type = "Treated vs never treated", k = k, l = NA, dd = dd, w = w)
    }
    for (j in seq_along(grps)) if (grps[j] > k) {
      l <- grps[j]; gl <- !is.na(d[[gvar]]) & d[[gvar]] == l
      nkl <- nk[i] / (nk[i] + nk[j]); Dk <- Dbar[i]; Dl <- Dbar[j]
      dd1 <- (m(gk, c(k, l - 1)) - m(gk, c(t0, k - 1))) - (m(gl, c(k, l - 1)) - m(gl, c(t0, k - 1)))
      w1 <- ((nk[i] + nk[j]) * (1 - Dl))^2 * nkl * (1 - nkl) * ((Dk - Dl) / (1 - Dl)) * ((1 - Dk) / (1 - Dl)) / VD
      dd2 <- (m(gl, c(l, tmax)) - m(gl, c(k, l - 1))) - (m(gk, c(l, tmax)) - m(gk, c(k, l - 1)))
      w2 <- ((nk[i] + nk[j]) * Dk)^2 * nkl * (1 - nkl) * (Dl / Dk) * ((Dk - Dl) / Dk) / VD
      out[[length(out) + 1]] <- data.frame(type = "Earlier treated vs later control", k = k, l = l, dd = dd1, w = w1)
      out[[length(out) + 1]] <- data.frame(type = "Later treated vs earlier control", k = k, l = l, dd = dd2, w = w2)
    }
  }
  do.call(rbind, out)
}
bysum <- function(x) do.call(rbind, lapply(split(x, x$type), function(z) data.frame(type = z$type[1], weight = sum(z$w), avg = sum(z$w * z$dd) / sum(z$w))))
```

## Where we left off

- Lecture 7a: difference-in-differences is **four averages and three subtractions**.
- It identifies the ATT if the two groups' untreated outcomes would have moved in parallel, and the baseline is untreated.
- Three regressions gave the same number: the interaction, two-way fixed effects (TWFE), the long difference. "DiD" and "TWFE" were synonyms.

\vspace{0.5em}

- That equivalence holds for **one** treated group, **one** control group and **one** date.
- This lecture and the next ask what happens when the design stops being a single $2 \times 2$.


## Four ways the single $2 \times 2$ breaks

1. **The sample changes under your feet.** Units drop out; a repeated cross-section draws different people.
2. **The trends are not parallel**, but a second comparison inside the same states might share the bias. *Triple differences.*
3. **The groups differ in ways you can measure.** Parallel trends holds only among similar units. *Covariates.*
4. **Treatment arrives at different dates.** TWFE quietly becomes a weighted average of comparisons nobody chose.

\vspace{0.5em}

- Today: what TWFE computes under staggered timing.
- Lecture 7c: estimators built to avoid its bad comparisons, and how to read their event studies.

# 1. Who Is in the Sample

## Imbalanced panels: is missing data a problem?

- A panel follows the same units. When some drop out or reappear, the panel is **imbalanced**.
- Parallel trends is a statement about the **average change** in $Y^0$. Missing units matter only if they change that average.
- If units go missing **at random**, the average is unaffected. <!-- (Wooldridge 2010).-->
- Weaker and enough: missingness $M$ is unrelated to the *untreated* outcome, given covariates,
$$
Y^0 \;\indep\; M \mid X \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \mathbb{E}[Y^0 \mid M=1, X] = \mathbb{E}[Y^0 \mid M=0, X].
$$

## Two people who leave

- **Maria** (treated) leaves because the training got her promoted.
  - She is missing because of her $Y^1$, not her $Y^0$.
  - The untreated trend is untouched. Her absence changes *which* treated outcomes we see, not the counterfactual.
- **Inez** (control) drops out in year 4, for reasons unrelated to $Y^0$ given $X$.
  - Impute her missing *observed* outcome from untreated units like her.
  - A missing-data problem, not an identification problem.

\vspace{0.4em}

- The rule: know **why** units are missing before you drop them.
<!-- - Chained DiD (Bellego, Benatia and Dortet-Bernadet 2024) links adjacent-period changes, under its own assumptions. -->

## Repeated cross-sections: did Napster kill music sales?

## Who is "treated" changes over time

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{lcccccccc}
\toprule
 & \multicolumn{2}{c}{1997} & \multicolumn{2}{c}{1998} & \multicolumn{2}{c}{1999} & \multicolumn{2}{c}{2000} \\
 & User & Non & User & Non & User & Non & User & Non \\
\midrule
Age & 40.2 & 49.0 & 42.3 & 49.0 & 44.1 & 49.4 & 44.3 & 49.9 \\
Income (\$000) & 52.9 & 30.5 & 52.0 & 26.2 & 50.0 & 26.6 & 47.5 & 26.3 \\
College graduate & 0.43 & 0.21 & 0.45 & 0.21 & 0.42 & 0.20 & 0.37 & 0.20 \\

\end{tabular}

- As internet use spread, the "treated" group got **older, poorer and less educated**.
- Older people buy less music. So users' spending falls even if Napster does nothing.
- Parallel trends breaks **because different people are sampled.**

<!-- 
## Why composition breaks parallel trends

Suppose spending depends on age, $Y^0 = a + bX + \text{trend}_t$. For the treated group,
$$
\bar Y_{T,\text{post}} - \bar Y_{T,\text{pre}} = \underbrace{\text{trend}}_{\text{same people, new year}} + \underbrace{b\,(\bar X_{T,\text{post}} - \bar X_{T,\text{pre}})}_{\text{different people}} .
$$

- The control group has its own composition term. DiD removes the trend, but not the **difference in composition terms**.
- In a panel the second term is zero by construction: the same people are followed.
- In a repeated cross-section it is zero only if each group's mix of $X$ is stable over time.
-->

## Diagnosing compositional change

- **Diagnostic 1.** A balance table *over time*, like the previous one, not just at baseline.
- **Diagnostic 2.** Run the DiD with an exogenous covariate as the *outcome*:
$$
X_{it} = \alpha + \beta_1 D_i + \beta_2 \text{Post}_t + \delta\,(D_i \times \text{Post}_t) + \varepsilon_{it}.
$$
- Napster cannot make anyone older. A significant $\hat\delta$ says the sample's composition shifted at treatment.
- If that $X$ also predicts $Y^0$, parallel trends is mechanically broken.

## Repairing it: reweight each period (Hong 2013)

1. Estimate **two** propensity scores, one per period:
$P_b = \Pr(D=1 \mid T=0, X)$ and $P_a = \Pr(D=1 \mid T=1, X)$.
2. Compute the four cell means with inverse-probability weights from **their own period's** score.
3. Take the $2 \times 2$ of the weighted means. Equivalently, the usual DiD regression by weighted least squares.

\vspace{0.4em}

- Intuition: reweight every year's sample to have the **same mix of $X$**. Then the composition term on the previous slide is zero.
- Panels are expensive; much of the world's data are repeated cross-sections. This fix deserves more use (see also Sant'Anna and Xu 2023).

# 2. Triple Differences

## Gruber (1994): who pays for maternity benefits?

- Some states mandated that employer health insurance cover maternity.
- If wages cannot adjust worker by worker, the mandate makes childbearing-age women more expensive to hire. Do their wages fall?
- The obvious DiD: married women aged 20--40, mandate states vs. other states, before vs. after. Writing $NJ$ for mandate states and $PA$ for the rest,
$$
\hat\delta = \underbrace{D}_{\text{effect}} + \underbrace{(NJ_t - PA_t)}_{\text{non-parallel trends bias}} .
$$
- Gruber worried that state labour markets were on different paths for reasons unrelated to the mandate. Then this DiD is biased.

## The fix: a second DiD in the same states

- Find a group in the **same states** that the law does not touch: single men aged 20--40 and workers over 40.
- Their DiD has no effect in it, only the bias: $\hat\delta_{\text{alt}} = (NJ_t - PA_t)$.
- Subtract:
$$
\hat\delta_{DDD} = \hat\delta_{\text{primary}} - \hat\delta_{\text{alt}} = D + (NJ_t - PA_t) - (NJ_t - PA_t) = D.
$$
- Intuition: the second DiD **measures the bias** of the first. Whatever made mandate states' labour markets drift, it shows up for the untouched workers too.

## Two biased DiDs, one unbiased triple difference

```{r ddd-sim}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.3
#| out-width: 84%
#| fig-align: center
# 40 states (20 with a mandate), two groups, 2010-2019. Mandate states drift down 500 a year for BOTH groups;
# the mandate lowers married women's earnings by 5,000 from 2015.
set.seed(3)
S <- 40; yrs <- 2010:2019
dd <- expand.grid(i = 1:100, g = 0:1, s = 1:S, year = yrs)
dd$ts <- as.numeric(dd$s <= S / 2); dd$tg <- dd$ts * dd$g
dd$y <- 30000 + rnorm(S, 0, 2000)[dd$s] - 3000 * dd$g + 400 * (dd$year - 2010) -
  500 * (dd$year - 2014) * dd$ts - 5000 * dd$tg * (dd$year >= 2015) + rnorm(nrow(dd), 0, 2000)
es1 <- feols(y ~ i(year, ts, ref = 2014) | s + year, dd[dd$g == 1, ], cluster = ~s)
es0 <- feols(y ~ i(year, ts, ref = 2014) | s + year, dd[dd$g == 0, ], cluster = ~s)
es3 <- feols(y ~ i(year, tg, ref = 2014) | s^g + s^year + g^year, dd, cluster = ~s)
grab <- function(e, v) { nm <- paste0("year::", yrs, ":", v); b <- coef(e)[nm]; s <- se(e)[nm]
  b[is.na(b)] <- 0; s[is.na(s)] <- 0; cbind(b, s) }
L <- list(grab(es1, "ts"), grab(es0, "ts"), grab(es3, "tg"))
cols <- c("black", "firebrick", "darkgreen"); pch <- c(16, 17, 15); off <- c(-0.12, 0, 0.12)
par(mar = c(2.6, 4.4, 0.3, 0.3), mgp = c(1.7, 0.5, 0), cex = 0.9, las = 1)
plot(NA, xlim = c(2009.7, 2019.3), ylim = range(sapply(L, function(m) range(m[, 1] + c(-2, 2) * m[, 2]))), xlab = "year", ylab = "", xaxt = "n")
axis(1, yrs); mtext("coefficient", 2, 3.3, las = 0, cex = 0.9)
abline(h = 0, col = "grey50"); abline(h = -5000, col = "grey60", lty = 3); abline(v = 2014.5, lty = 2, col = "grey50")
for (j in 1:3) { x <- yrs + off[j]; m <- L[[j]]
  segments(x, m[, 1] - 1.96 * m[, 2], x, m[, 1] + 1.96 * m[, 2], col = cols[j]); points(x, m[, 1], pch = pch[j], col = cols[j]) }
text(2018.6, -4550, "true effect = -5,000", cex = 0.8, col = "grey30")
legend("bottomleft", bty = "n", pch = pch, col = cols, cex = 0.85,
  legend = c("DiD, married women 20-40 (biased)", "DiD, untouched workers (same bias)", "triple difference"))
```
\src{Simulated, after Cunningham (2025), Figure 10.3: both groups share a bias of $-500$ a year; true effect $-5{,}000$.}

- Both DiDs show the same falling pre-trend. Their difference (green) is flat before and $-5{,}000$ after.

## The assumption: parallel bias

- With $D$ the state and $G$ the eligible group, DDD needs the **same bias** for both groups (Olden and Møen 2022):
$$
\begin{aligned}
&\mathbb{E}[\Delta Y^0 \mid D=1, G=1] - \mathbb{E}[\Delta Y^0 \mid D=0, G=1] \\
&\qquad = \mathbb{E}[\Delta Y^0 \mid D=1, G=0] - \mathbb{E}[\Delta Y^0 \mid D=0, G=0].
\end{aligned}
$$
- The second DiD is **not required to be zero**, only equal to the first DiD's bias.
- If it *were* zero, the first DiD was fine all along. The second group would then be a falsification ("same outcome, different group"), as with Miller, Johnson and Wherry's elderly in 7a.
- So triple differences is a **design**, not a falsification.

## Triple differences by regression

Eight averages and seven subtractions. Identical to OLS with **all** interactions of period $\tau_t$, group $\delta_g$ and state $D_i$:
$$
\begin{aligned}
Y_{igt} = \alpha &+ \beta_1\tau_t + \beta_2 \delta_g + \beta_3 D_i + \beta_4(\delta\tau)_{gt} \\
&+ \beta_5(\tau D)_{ti} + \beta_6(\delta D)_{ig} + \beta_7(\delta \tau D)_{igt} + \varepsilon_{igt}.
\end{aligned}
$$

- $\beta_7$ is the triple difference. Drop any of the two-way terms and it no longer is.
- Event study: interact the two- and three-way terms with every period except $\tau = -1$.

## Triple differences in practice

- **Cluster** where the law varies: the state.
- **Show three event studies**: each DiD, and their difference.
- The two DiDs' pre-trends should look alike. That is the visible part of "parallel bias".
- Almost nobody shows them. Show yours.

\midrule
\multicolumn{4}{l}{\emph{A. Married women 20--40}} \\
Experimental states & 1.547 & 1.513 & $-0.034$ \\
Non-experimental states & 1.369 & 1.397 & $0.028$ \\
Difference-in-differences & & & $\mathbf{-0.062}$ (0.022) \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{4}{l}{\emph{B. Over 40 and single men 20--40}} \\
Experimental states & 1.759 & 1.748 & $-0.011$ \\
Non-experimental states & 1.630 & 1.627 & $-0.003$ \\
Difference-in-differences & & & $\mathbf{-0.008}$ (0.014) \\

- Panel B *estimates the bias* of panel A. Here it is small, so DDD and DiD nearly agree.
- Married women's wages fell about $5$ percent: the mandate was paid for by the workers it protected.
- No event study in 1994; the practice did not arrive until the 2000s.

# 3. Covariates

## Levels, trends, and why covariates enter

- Parallel trends is about trends, not levels. Groups at different levels are fine **in principle**.
- In practice a large level gap is a warning: whatever made the groups different might also make their untreated *trends* different.
- Kahn-Lang and Lang (2020): every DiD paper should say why the levels differ and why that would not affect the trends.
- Often the **distribution of covariates** drives both. Then condition on them, **conditional parallel trends** (Heckman, Ichimura and Todd 1997):
$$
\mathbb{E}[Y^0_{\text{post}} - Y^0_{\text{pre}} \mid D=1, X] \;=\; \mathbb{E}[Y^0_{\text{post}} - Y^0_{\text{pre}} \mid D=0, X].
$$

## What conditioning buys, and what it costs

- **Buys**: parallel trends only among units with the **same $X$**. Young treated workers are compared with young controls, old with old.
- **Costs** two things:
  - **common support**: for every treated $X$ there must be controls with that $X$, or a functional form that extrapolates where there are none;
  - a decision about **which** $X$.

\vspace{0.4em}

- Example: if young workers' earnings grow faster and the treated are mostly young, the raw DiD mixes the treatment effect with an age-driven trend. Conditioning on age removes the age-driven part.

## Which covariates?

```{r dag-x}
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 1.5
#| out-width: 40%
#| fig-align: center
par(mar = rep(0.2, 4), cex = 1.15)
plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(0, 4), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "")
text(5, 3.4, expression("covariates " * X)); text(1.5, 0.6, expression(D)); text(8.5, 0.6, expression(E * "[" * Delta * Y^0 * "]"))
arrows(4.3, 2.9, 2.0, 1.0, length = 0.1, lwd = 1.5); arrows(5.7, 2.9, 7.9, 1.0, length = 0.1, lwd = 1.5)
```
\src{After Cunningham (2025), Figure 10.4.}

$X$ must do **both** things:

1. $X \rightarrow D$: it is distributed differently in treated and control groups;
2. $X \rightarrow \Delta \mathbb{E}[Y^0]$: it drives the untreated **trend**.

- Only the first: harmless but useless. Only the second: precision, not identification. Both: a confounder of trends.

## Where the list comes from

- **The field** that studies ordinary trends in your outcome.
- **A DAG** that forces you to say what moves $Y^0$.
- **Data-driven selection** fitted **on untreated units only**; Borgschulte and Vogler (2020) use LASSO this way.

\vspace{0.4em}

- **Never** a post-treatment covariate: it may respond to treatment. Measure $X$ at baseline.
- The list can swing the estimate a lot. Fix it before you see results, and say so.

## Is there imbalance? The normalized difference

$$
\text{Norm.\ Diff}_\omega = \frac{\bar X_{\omega,T} - \bar X_{\omega,C}}{\sqrt{(S^2_{\omega,T} + S^2_{\omega,C})/2}}
$$

- A difference in means in standard-deviation units, so it does not grow with the sample the way a $t$-statistic does.
- Rule of thumb: worry when $|{\cdot}| > 0.25$ (Imbens and Rubin 2015).

## Imbalance in the LaLonde data

Lecture 3's job-training data, treated vs. CPS controls:

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
 & Mean treated & Mean control & Norm.\ diff. \\
\midrule
Age & 25.8 & 33.2 & $-0.80$ \\
Education & 10.3 & 12.0 & $-0.68$ \\
Black & 0.84 & 0.07 & $2.43$ \\
Hispanic & 0.06 & 0.07 & $-0.05$ \\
Married & 0.19 & 0.71 & $-1.23$ \\
Unemployed 1974 & 0.71 & 0.12 & $1.49$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

- Everything but Hispanic is far past the line.
- Irrelevant if these variables do not drive earnings *trends*; fatal if they do. Either way, use conditional parallel trends and an estimator built for it.

## Four ways to use conditional parallel trends

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{lll}
\toprule
Estimator & What it does & What must be right \\
\midrule
IPW (Abadie 2005) & reweights controls to look like the treated & the propensity score \\
Outcome regression & predicts the treated's $\Delta Y^0$ from controls & the outcome model \\
Doubly robust & both at once & either one of the two \\
TWFE $+\,\theta X$ & adds $X$ linearly to the regression & linearity, constant $\theta$, \\
 & & homogeneous effects \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

- All four target the same thing: the **counterfactual change** of the treated, built from controls with the same $X$.
- They differ in which side they adjust and what model they trust.

## Estimator 1: inverse probability weighting (Abadie 2005)

Estimate $p(X) = \Pr(D=1 \mid X_b)$ from **baseline** covariates. Then
$$
\hat\delta_{IPW} = \mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{Y_{\text{post}} - Y_{\text{pre}}}{\Pr(D=1)} \cdot \frac{D - p(X)}{1 - p(X)}\right].
$$

- Treated unit: weight $\dfrac{1 - p}{1 - p} = 1$. **Only the controls are reweighted.**
- Control unit: weight $-\dfrac{p}{1-p}$, the odds of being treated.
- Intuition: a control that *looks like* a treated unit ($p$ near 1) counts a lot; one that looks nothing like them ($p$ near 0) barely counts.

## IPW by hand

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{lcccrr}
\toprule
 & $\Delta Y$ & $D$ & $p(X)$ & weight & weighted $\Delta Y$ \\
\midrule
Pat & 45 & 0 & 0.75 & $-3$ & $-135$ \\
Tiffany & 100 & 1 & 0.90 & $1$ & $100$ \\
Dolores & 42 & 0 & 0.25 & $-1/3$ & $-14$ \\
Danny & 75 & 1 & 0.50 & $1$ & $75$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

- Pat looks like the treated ($p = 0.75$): he counts **three times**. Dolores ($p = 0.25$) counts a third.
- The formula: $\tfrac14(100 + 75 - 135 - 14) / 0.5 = 13$. With weights normalized to sum to one, as in the doubly robust formula below: $87.5 - \tfrac{135 + 14}{3 + 1/3} = 42.8$. The two agree in large samples, not in a sample of four.

## IPW: assumptions and the outlier that matters

- Assumptions: no anticipation, conditional parallel trends, common support, a **correctly specified score**.
- An "outlier" in IPW is not an extreme outcome but an **extreme weight**.
- A control with $p = 0.99991$ gets weight $-0.99991/0.00009 \approx -11{,}110$. One unit can move the whole estimate.
- Before estimating, **count** the controls with scores near one. Trim if you must.
- A histogram of scores checks overlap, but often hides a handful of explosive weights; counting does not.

## Estimator 2: outcome regression (Heckman, Ichimura and Todd 1997)

- The mirror image. Using **controls only**, fit the change in outcomes on baseline covariates: $\hat\mu(X)$ predicts $\Delta Y^0$ from $X$.
- Apply it to each treated unit's $X$ to impute its counterfactual change:
$$
\hat\delta_{OR} = \big(\bar Y_{1,\text{post}} - \bar Y_{1,\text{pre}}\big) - \frac{1}{n_T}\sum_{i: D_i = 1}\big[\hat\mu_{0,\text{post}}(X_i) - \hat\mu_{0,\text{pre}}(X_i)\big].
$$
- Why it works: under conditional parallel trends, the controls' relationship between $\Delta Y^0$ and $X$ is the treated group's too. That is the whole content of the assumption.
- Assumptions: the same three, plus a **correctly specified outcome model**.

## IPW and outcome regression: two sides of one subtraction

$$
\text{ATT} = \underbrace{\mathbb{E}[\Delta Y \mid D=1]}_{\text{observed}} - \underbrace{\mathbb{E}[\Delta Y^0 \mid D=1]}_{\text{must be built from controls}}
$$

- **IPW** builds the second term by **reweighting controls** until their $X$ looks like the treated group's. It models *who gets treated*.
- **Outcome regression** builds it by **predicting** from a model fitted on controls. It models *how outcomes move*.
- IPW leaves the treated alone; OR leaves the controls' weights alone. Different transformations, same target.

## Estimator 3: doubly robust (Sant'Anna and Zhao 2020)

Reweight the controls with the score **and** subtract the outcome-model prediction from everyone:
$$
\hat\delta_{DR} = \mathbb{E}\!\left[\left(\frac{D}{\mathbb{E}[D]} - \frac{\frac{p(X)(1-D)}{1-p(X)}}{\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{p(X)(1-D)}{1-p(X)}\right]}\right)\big(\Delta Y - \hat\mu_{0,\Delta}(X)\big)\right].
$$

- Consistent if **either** the score or the outcome model is right. You are allowed to be wrong once.
- Intuition: if the outcome model is right, $\Delta Y - \hat\mu$ is pure noise for controls, so any weights work. If the score is right, the weights fix whatever the outcome model got wrong.
- Lecture 3b showed why the repair term cancels. Here the outcome is a *change*. Chang (2020) uses machine-learned nuisance functions.

## Estimator 4: the regression everyone runs

$$
Y_{it} = \alpha_1 + \alpha_2\,\text{Post}_t + \alpha_3 D_i + \delta\,(D_i \times \text{Post}_t) + \theta X_{it} + \varepsilon_{it}
$$

- Nothing stops you. But two more assumptions hide in $\theta X_{it}$:
  1. **homogeneous effects** across $X$;
  2. **no covariate-specific trends**.
- Plus functional form: nothing forces common support, so the line extrapolates.

## Hidden assumption 1: homogeneous effects

Let $X$ affect $Y^1$ by $\theta_1$ and $Y^0$ by $\theta_2$. Then
$$
\text{ATT}(X) = \mathbb{E}[Y^1_{\text{post}} - Y^0_{\text{post}} \mid D=1, X] = \delta + (\theta_1 - \theta_2)X .
$$

- The regression reports $\delta$, which is the ATT only if $\theta_1 = \theta_2$.
- In words: the same treatment effect for old and young, rich and poor.
- Ask it concretely. Is the age--earnings profile the same with and without a degree? If not, the assumption fails.

## Hidden assumption 2: no covariate-specific trends

With cell means $\bar X_{dt}$ (group $d$, period $t$), the DiD of the cells is
$$
\delta^{DD} = \delta + \theta(\bar X_{11} - \bar X_{10}) - \theta(\bar X_{01} - \bar X_{00}).
$$

- The regression imposes **one $\theta$ in every period**.
- If the **return** to $X$ changes over time (say, the college premium rises), or $X$ trends differently across groups, the extra terms do not cancel.
- Conditional parallel trends allows both. The additive regression assumes them away.

## The four estimators, simulated

```{r cov-sim}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 2.4
#| out-width: 80%
#| fig-align: center
one <- function(n = 1000) {
  age <- runif(n, 20, 40); gpa <- runif(n, 1, 4)
  D <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-6 + 0.15 * age + 0.6 * gpa))
  fe <- rnorm(n, 0, 500)
  y0_pre  <- fe + 100 * age + 1000 * gpa + rnorm(n, 0, 1500)
  y0_post <- fe + 1000 + 200 * age + 2000 * gpa + rnorm(n, 0, 1500)      # return to X changes over time
  y1_post <- y0_post + 1000 + 100 * (age - 30) + 500 * (gpa - 2.5)       # effect varies with X
  y_post <- ifelse(D == 1, y1_post, y0_post); dy <- y_post - y0_pre
  att <- mean((y1_post - y0_post)[D == 1])
  long <- data.frame(y = c(y0_pre, y_post), post = rep(0:1, each = n), D = rep(D, 2), age = rep(age, 2), gpa = rep(gpa, 2))
  twfe <- coef(lm(y ~ D * post + age + gpa, long))["D:post"]
  p <- fitted(glm(D ~ age + gpa + I(age^2) + I(gpa^2), family = binomial))
  ipw <- sum(ifelse(D == 1, 1, -p / (1 - p)) * dy) / sum(D)
  mu <- predict(lm(dy ~ age + gpa + I(age^2) + I(gpa^2), subset = D == 0), newdata = data.frame(age, gpa))
  or <- mean(dy[D == 1]) - mean(mu[D == 1])
  w0 <- p * (1 - D) / (1 - p)
  dr <- sum(D * (dy - mu)) / sum(D) - sum(w0 * (dy - mu)) / sum(w0)
  c(TWFE = twfe - att, IPW = ipw - att, OR = or - att, DR = dr - att)
}
set.seed(7); R <- t(replicate(400, one()))
par(mar = c(2.6, 4.6, 0.3, 0.3), mgp = c(1.7, 0.5, 0), cex = 0.9)
dens <- lapply(1:4, function(j) density(R[, j]))
plot(NA, xlim = range(R), ylim = c(0, max(sapply(dens, function(d) max(d$y)))), xlab = "estimate minus ATT", ylab = "", las = 1)
mtext("density", side = 2, line = 3.4, cex = 0.9)
cols <- c("firebrick", "grey40", "steelblue", "darkgreen"); ltys <- c(1, 2, 1, 3)
for (j in 1:4) lines(dens[[j]], col = cols[j], lwd = 2, lty = ltys[j])
abline(v = 0, col = "grey60")
legend("topleft", bty = "n", lwd = 2, col = cols, lty = ltys, cex = 0.9, legend = c("TWFE with additive X", "IPW", "Outcome regression", "Doubly robust"))
```

- Treatment depends on age and GPA; so does the untreated trend, with the **return** to each doubling over time; the effect varies with both. Conditional parallel trends holds and both nuisance models are correct.

## Reading the simulation

- Two periods, $1{,}000$ units, $400$ replications.
- Mean bias: TWFE $`r round(mean(R[,1]))`$; IPW $`r round(mean(R[,2]))`$; OR $`r round(mean(R[,3]))`$; DR $`r round(mean(R[,4]))`$.
- Standard deviations $`r round(sd(R[,1]))`$, $`r round(sd(R[,2]))`$, $`r round(sd(R[,3]))`$, $`r round(sd(R[,4]))`$: IPW pays in variance for controls with high scores.

\vspace{0.4em}

- The problem is not regression but the **additive, time-constant** way this specification lets $X$ in. TWFE violates both hidden assumptions here.
- Wooldridge (2021) fixes it within OLS, by interacting $X$ with treatment and time; the other three fix it by construction.

# 4. Differential Timing and Two-Way Fixed Effects

## When "Post" has no meaning

Card and Krueger again, but suppose New York also raised its minimum wage, in 1993.

\begin{center}\scriptsize
\begin{tabular}{lccc|lccc|lccc}
\toprule
Year & State & Treat & Post & Year & State & Treat & Post & Year & State & Treat & Post \\
\midrule
1991 & NJ & 1 & 0 & 1991 & NY & 1 & 0 & 1991 & PA & 0 & 0 \\
1992 & NJ & 1 & 1 & 1992 & NY & 1 & 0 & 1992 & PA & 0 & ? \\
1993 & NJ & 1 & 1 & 1993 & NY & 1 & 1 & 1993 & PA & 0 & ? \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

- Is Pennsylvania's "Post" relative to 1992 or 1993? The interaction regression cannot even be written down.
- So everyone runs the version that can:
$$
Y_{ist} = \beta_0 + \delta D_{ist} + \tau_t + \sigma_s + \varepsilon_{ist}, \qquad D_{ist} = \mathbf{1}\{\text{unit } s \text{ is treated at } t\}.
$$
- Coding $D$ is trivial. The question is what $\hat\delta^{TWFE}$ *is*, in potential outcomes.

## What does TWFE average?

- By Frisch--Waugh--Lovell, $\hat\delta^{TWFE}$ is the slope of $Y$ on $D$ after both are demeaned by unit and by period:
$$
\hat\delta = \frac{\sum_{s,t} \tilde D_{st}\tilde Y_{st}}{\sum_{s,t} \tilde D_{st}^2}.
$$
- Goodman-Bacon (2021): this slope is **exactly** a weighted average of all the simple $2 \times 2$ DiDs in the data.
- A warm-up: the average of $4$, $10$ and $3$ is $5.67$, weight $\tfrac13$ each. If TWFE averages nine $2 \times 2$'s, are the weights $\tfrac19$?
- No. OLS picks weights that are best for **predicting** $Y$, not for averaging treatment effects (Słoczyński 2022).

## Nine $2 \times 2$'s from three timing groups

Groups $a$ (treated 1980), $b$ (1983), $c$ (1986), and a never-treated group $U$:

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{ccc}
\toprule
$a$ vs $b$ & $b$ vs $a$ & $c$ vs $a$ \\
$a$ vs $c$ & $b$ vs $c$ & $c$ vs $b$ \\
$a$ vs $U$ & $b$ vs $U$ & $c$ vs $U$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

- **Bottom row**: never-treated control. Fine.
- **Left of the diagonal** ($a$ vs $b$, $a$ vs $c$, $b$ vs $c$): the control is **not yet treated** during the window. Fine.
- **Upper right** ($b$ vs $a$, $c$ vs $a$, $c$ vs $b$): the control was **already treated**. Three of the nine. Nobody chose them; OLS did.

## The four kinds of $2 \times 2$, drawn

```{r four-2x2}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| out-width: 80%
#| fig-align: center
tt <- 0:100; k <- 34; l <- 85
yk <- 18 + 0.1 * tt + 10 * (tt >= k); yl <- 10 + 0.1 * tt + 15 * (tt >= l); yU <- 5 + 0.1 * tt
panel <- function(title, on, win, marks, spans) {
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 100), ylim = c(-4, 42), xaxt = "n", xlab = "", ylab = "y", main = title, font.main = 1, cex.main = 0.95)
  axis(1, at = marks, labels = names(marks))
  w <- tt >= win[1] & tt <= win[2]; ev <- tt %% 3 == 0
  for (g in c("U", "k", "l")) {
    y <- switch(g, k = yk, l = yl, U = yU); is_on <- g %in% on
    col <- if (is_on) c(k = "black", l = "steelblue", U = "grey35")[g] else "grey80"
    ww <- if (is_on) w else rep(TRUE, length(tt))
    lines(tt[ww], y[ww], col = col, lwd = if (g == "U") 3 else 1.2)
    if (g != "U") points(tt[ww & ev], y[ww & ev], pch = if (g == "k") 17 else 1, col = col, cex = 0.7)
  }
  abline(v = marks, col = "firebrick")
  for (s in spans) { arrows(s[[1]], 0.5, s[[2]], 0.5, code = 3, length = 0.06); text(mean(c(s[[1]], s[[2]])), -2.3, s[[3]], font = 3, cex = 0.8) }
}
par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(2.2, 2.8, 1.6, 0.4), mgp = c(1.5, 0.45, 0), cex = 0.8, las = 1)
panel("A. Early group vs. untreated group", c("k", "U"), c(0, 100), c(k = k), list(list(0, k, "PRE(k)"), list(k, 100, "POST(k)")))
panel("B. Late group vs. untreated group", c("l", "U"), c(0, 100), c(l = l), list(list(0, l, "PRE(l)"), list(l, 100, "POST(l)")))
panel("C. Early vs. late group, before l", c("k", "l"), c(0, l - 1), c(k = k, l = l), list(list(0, k, "PRE(k)"), list(k, l, "MID(k,l)")))
panel("D. Late vs. early group, after k", c("k", "l"), c(k, 100), c(k = k, l = l), list(list(k, l, "MID(k,l)"), list(l, 100, "POST(l)")))
legend("topleft", bty = "n", cex = 0.85, pch = c(17, 1, NA), lwd = c(1.2, 1.2, 3), col = c("black", "steelblue", "grey35"),
  legend = c("early group k", "late group l", "never treated U"))
```
\src{After Goodman-Bacon (2021), Figure 1, and Cunningham (2025), Figure 10.6. Grey: the group not used in that $2 \times 2$.}

## Reading the four panels

- **A. Early vs. untreated.** $k$ before and after its date, against $U$. The 7a design.
- **B. Late vs. untreated.** The same for $l$.
- **C. Early vs. late, before $l$.** $l$ is still untreated during the window *mid*$(k,l)$: a **not-yet-treated** control. Legal.
- **D. Late vs. early, after $k$.** $l$ switches on; $k$ is already treated throughout. The **already-treated** control: the "forbidden comparison" (Borusyak, Jaravel and Spiess).

\vspace{0.4em}

- In panel D, both of $k$'s windows are $Y^1$. Any change in $k$'s *effect* between the windows looks like a change in the counterfactual.

## The three kinds, as formulas

$$
\begin{aligned}
\hat\delta^{2\times2}_{kU} &= (\bar y_k^{\,post(k)} - \bar y_k^{\,pre(k)}) - (\bar y_U^{\,post(k)} - \bar y_U^{\,pre(k)}) &&\text{never-treated control} \\[2pt]
\hat\delta^{2\times2}_{kl} &= (\bar y_k^{\,mid} - \bar y_k^{\,pre(k)}) - (\bar y_l^{\,mid} - \bar y_l^{\,pre(k)}) &&\text{not-yet-treated control} \\[2pt]
\hat\delta^{2\times2}_{lk} &= (\bar y_l^{\,post(l)} - \bar y_l^{\,mid}) - (\bar y_k^{\,post(l)} - \bar y_k^{\,mid}) &&\text{already-treated control}
\end{aligned}
$$

- Each is four averages and three subtractions; only the windows and the control group change.
- Substitute potential outcomes. The first two give an ATT plus the usual parallel-trends bias.

## Why the third is forbidden

With no anticipation, as in 7a:
$$
\hat\delta^{2\times2}_{lk} = \text{ATT}_l(post) + \text{PT bias} - \underbrace{\big[\text{ATT}_k(post(l)) - \text{ATT}_k(mid)\big]}_{\text{growth in } k\text{'s own effect}} .
$$

- The control $k$ is treated in both windows. Its outcome rises if its **effect** grows, and that rise is subtracted from $l$'s estimate.
- If $k$'s effect is constant, the bracket is zero: a treated control whose effect does not move differences out like a fixed effect.
- "Forbidden comparison" is Borusyak, Jaravel and Spiess's phrase. de Chaisemartin and D'Haultfoeuille (2020), Goodman-Bacon (2021) and Sun and Abraham (2021) found the problem independently, within a few years.

## The forbidden comparison in numbers

Both groups have flat $Y^0$. Group $k$ is treated at $t = 2$, with an effect of $10$ that grows by $10$ a year. Group $l$ is treated at $t = 4$, with a constant effect of $5$.

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
 & \multicolumn{2}{c}{\emph{mid}: $t = 2, 3$} & \multicolumn{2}{c}{\emph{post}$(l)$: $t = 4, 5$} \\
\midrule
$l$ (treated in the window) & 0 & 0 & 5 & 5 \\
$k$ (the "control") & 10 & 20 & 30 & 40 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

- $l$'s change: $5 - 0 = 5$. $k$'s change: $35 - 15 = 20$.
- The $2 \times 2$: $5 - 20 = \mathbf{-15}$. The true effect is $+5$.
- Parallel trends holds exactly. The control is not wrong about $Y^0$; it is contaminated by its **own growing effect**.

## The weights: group size times treatment variance

$$
\hat\delta^{TWFE} = \sum_{k \ne U} s_{kU}\,\hat\delta^{2\times2}_{kU} + \sum_{k \ne U}\sum_{l > k}\big[s^{k}_{kl}\,\hat\delta^{2\times2,k}_{kl} + s^{l}_{kl}\,\hat\delta^{2\times2,l}_{lk}\big], \qquad \sum s = 1,
$$
$$
s_{kU} = \frac{(n_k + n_U)^2\; n_{kU}(1 - n_{kU})\; \bar D_k(1 - \bar D_k)}{\widehat{\text{Var}}(\tilde D)}, \quad n_{kU} = \frac{n_k}{n_k + n_U}.
$$

- Similar formulas for the timing pairs. Every weight is **positive**, and they come from two ingredients:
  - **sample shares** $n_k$: bigger groups count more, as you would expect;
  - **treatment variance** $\bar D_k(1-\bar D_k)$, where $\bar D_k$ is the share of the panel a group spends treated.

## Treatment variance favours the middle

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
 & New Jersey & New York \\
\midrule
Treated from & 1992 & 1993 \\
Years treated, 1990--95 & 4 of 6 & 3 of 6 \\
$\bar D$ & 0.67 & 0.50 \\
$\bar D(1 - \bar D)$ & 0.22 & \textbf{0.25} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r var-curve}
#| fig-width: 4.2
#| fig-height: 2.8
#| out-width: 72%
#| fig-align: center
par(mar = c(2.6, 3.4, 0.6, 0.4), mgp = c(1.7, 0.5, 0), cex = 0.9, las = 1)
curve(x * (1 - x), 0, 1, lwd = 2, xlab = expression("share of panel treated, " * bar(D)), ylab = "", ylim = c(0, 0.27), yaxs = "i")
mtext(expression(bar(D) * (1 - bar(D))), 2, 2.4, las = 0, cex = 0.9)
segments(0.5, 0, 0.5, 0.25, lty = 2, col = "grey50"); segments(0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.25, lty = 2, col = "grey50")
points(c(2/3, 0.5), c(2/9, 0.25), pch = 16, col = c("firebrick", "steelblue"))
text(2/3, 2/9, "NJ", pos = 4, col = "firebrick", cex = 0.85); text(0.5, 0.25, "NY", pos = 3, col = "steelblue", cex = 0.85, offset = 0.3)
```
\src{After Cunningham (2025), Figure 10.7.}
:::
::::

- $\bar D(1-\bar D)$ peaks at $\bar D = 0.5$: $0.1 \times 0.9 = 0.09$, $0.4 \times 0.6 = 0.24$, $0.5 \times 0.5 = 0.25$.
- TWFE **over-weights groups treated near the middle of the panel** and under-weights early and late adopters. Not because their comparisons are better, but because OLS likes variance.
- Change the panel's start or end date and the weights change with it.

## From arithmetic to causality

Replace each $2 \times 2$ by its potential-outcome content, with no anticipation:
$$
\operatorname{plim}\hat\delta^{TWFE} \;=\; \text{VWATT} \;+\; \text{VWPT} \;-\; \Delta\text{ATT}.
$$

- **VWATT**: a variance-weighted average of group ATTs. Causal, but weighted by the panel's dates rather than by anything you chose.
- **VWPT**: variance-weighted parallel-trends bias. Zero if parallel trends holds for every pair.
- $\boldsymbol{\Delta}$**ATT**: the already-treated controls' *change* in effect, with a **minus sign**. Zero only if effects are constant over time.

\vspace{0.3em}

- So parallel trends is **not enough** for this regression. You also need effects that do not change over time.

## Constant effects vs. dynamic effects

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r eff-const}
#| fig-width: 3.8
#| fig-height: 2.6
#| out-width: 74%
#| fig-align: center
eff_plot <- function(dyn) {
  par(mar = c(1.8, 1.8, 0.4, 0.4), mgp = c(0.6, 0, 0), cex = 0.85)
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(0, 10), axes = FALSE, xlab = "time", ylab = expression(Y^0 * ", " * Y^1)); box(bty = "l")
  abline(v = 5, lty = 2, col = "grey60")
  segments(0, 3, 5, 3, lwd = 2); segments(5, 3, 9, 3, lty = 2, lwd = 2, col = "grey60")
  y1 <- function(x) if (dyn) 5 + 1.1 * (x - 5) else 7
  segments(5, y1(5), 9, y1(9), lwd = 2)
  for (x in c(6, 8)) arrows(x, 3, x, y1(x), code = 3, length = 0.07, col = "grey40", lty = if (x == 8) 3 else 1)
  text(6, 3 + (y1(6) - 3) / 2, expression(ATT[1]), pos = 4, cex = 0.85); text(8, 3 + (y1(8) - 3) / 2, expression(ATT[2]), pos = 4, cex = 0.85)
  text(9.3, y1(9) + 0.35, expression(E(Y^1)), cex = 0.8); text(9.4, 3.4, expression(E(Y^0)), col = "grey50", cex = 0.8)
}
eff_plot(FALSE)
```
\begin{center}\footnotesize Constant: $\text{ATT}_1 = \text{ATT}_2$, $\Delta\text{ATT} = 0$\end{center}
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r eff-dyn}
#| fig-width: 3.8
#| fig-height: 2.6
#| out-width: 74%
#| fig-align: center
eff_plot(TRUE)
```
\begin{center}\footnotesize Dynamic: $\text{ATT}_2 > \text{ATT}_1$, $\Delta\text{ATT} > 0$\end{center}
:::
::::
\src{After Cunningham (2025), Figures 10.8 and 10.9.}

- Under parallel trends, $\hat\delta^{TWFE} = \text{VWATT} - \Delta\text{ATT}$. If effects grow, TWFE is biased **toward zero**.
- $\text{VWATT} = 10$, $\Delta\text{ATT} = 3$: estimate $7$. $\Delta\text{ATT} = 11$: estimate $-1$. **The sign flips.**

## The Baker simulation: the truth

```{r baker-raw}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 2.3
#| out-width: 76%
#| fig-align: center
mt <- with(b, tapply(y, list(year, group), mean))
par(mar = c(2.6, 3.2, 0.3, 0.3), mgp = c(1.7, 0.5, 0), cex = 0.9)
matplot(1980:2009, mt, type = "l", lty = 1, lwd = 2, col = c("black", "firebrick", "steelblue", "darkgreen"), xlab = "year", ylab = "mean outcome", las = 1)
abline(v = c(1986, 1992, 1998, 2004) - 0.5, col = "grey70", lty = 3)
legend("topleft", bty = "n", lwd = 2, col = c("black", "firebrick", "steelblue", "darkgreen"), cex = 0.85, legend = c("treated 1986", "treated 1992", "treated 1998", "treated 2004"))
```

- $1{,}000$ firms, $1980$--$2009$, four equal cohorts treated in $1986$, $1992$, $1998$, $2004$.
- Every firm's $Y^0$ grows by $1$ a year plus noise: parallel trends holds **firm by firm**. No anticipation, no omitted variables.

## The Baker simulation: two outcomes

- **Constant** effects: $10$, $8$, $6$, $4$ by cohort, forever.
- **Dynamic** effects (the figure): the same numbers, **added again every year** treated.
  - The 1986 cohort: $10$ in 1986, $20$ in 1987, ..., $240$ by 2009.
  - The 2004 cohort: $4$, $8$, ..., $24$ by 2009.

\vspace{0.4em}

- Every effect is positive. Every textbook assumption holds.
- Question: what does the regression everyone runs return?

## The Baker simulation: parameters and the regression

```{r baker-twfe}
tw_c <- feols(y2 ~ treat | id + year, b, cluster = ~id)
tw_d <- feols(y ~ treat | id + year, b, cluster = ~id)
bk <- bacon(b, "y"); bks <- bysum(bk)
bks_c <- bysum(bacon(b, "y2"))
```

\begin{center}\scriptsize
\begin{tabular}{lcccccc|c}
\toprule
 & ATT(1986) & ATT(1992) & ATT(1998) & ATT(2004) & Simple & Group & $\hat\delta^{TWFE}$ (s.e.) \\
\midrule
Constant & 10 & 8 & 6 & 4 & 8 & 7 & $`r f2(coef(tw_c))`$ ($`r f3(se(tw_c))`$) \\
Dynamic & 125 & 76 & 39 & 14 & 82 & 63.5 & $\mathbf{`r f2(coef(tw_d))`}$ ($`r f3(se(tw_d))`$) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

- *Simple ATT*: average over all treated firm-years. *Group ATT*: average of the four cohort averages. Both correct; they weight the cells differently.
- **Constant:** $\Delta\text{ATT} = 0$, so only the variance weights remain. The answer, $7$, is a VWATT: causal, though not the simple ATT.
- **Dynamic:** the regression returns $\mathbf{`r f2(coef(tw_d))`}$ with a $t$-statistic of $10$. **The sign is wrong.**

## The Baker simulation: inside the coefficient

Bacon's decomposition, computed by hand from group means, reproduces the coefficient exactly:

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
 & Weight & Average $2 \times 2$ \\
\midrule
Earlier treated vs later control (not-yet-treated) & $`r f2(bks$weight[1])`$ & $`r f1(bks$avg[1])`$ \\
Later treated vs earlier control (already-treated) & $`r f2(bks$weight[2])`$ & $`r f1(bks$avg[2])`$ \\
\midrule
$`r f2(bks$weight[1])` \times `r f1(bks$avg[1])` + `r f2(bks$weight[2])` \times (`r f1(bks$avg[2])`)$ & & $`r f2(sum(bks$weight * bks$avg))`$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

- No never-treated group, so all $`r nrow(bk)`$ $2 \times 2$'s compare two cohorts.
- Half the weight sits on comparisons whose control was **already treated and still climbing**. They average $`r f1(bks$avg[2])`$.

## Why constant effects were harmless

- Same decomposition, constant-effect outcome: the two halves average $`r f1(bks_c$avg[1])`$ and $`r f1(bks_c$avg[2])`$.
- A control whose effect does not move is just a level shift. The subtraction removes it, as a fixed effect would.
- With dynamic effects the control's outcome **keeps climbing**, and that climb is read as a counterfactual trend.

\vspace{0.4em}

- The weights are **observable**. Compute them for your design before deciding whether TWFE is good enough.
- Stata and R: `bacondecomp`.

## Bacon on real data: castle doctrine, all cohorts

```{r castle-bacon}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 2.3
#| out-width: 76%
#| fig-align: center
tw_cst <- feols(l_homicide ~ post | sid + year, cst, cluster = ~sid)
bc <- bacon(cst, "l_homicide", idvar = "sid", tvar = "year", gvar = "effyear"); bcs <- bysum(bc)
par(mar = c(2.6, 3.2, 0.3, 0.3), mgp = c(1.7, 0.5, 0), cex = 0.9)
pchs <- c("Earlier treated vs later control" = 1, "Later treated vs earlier control" = 4, "Treated vs never treated" = 16)
plot(bc$dd, bc$w, pch = pchs[bc$type], xlab = "2 x 2 estimate", ylab = "weight", las = 1, cex = 1.1)
abline(v = coef(tw_cst), col = "grey50", lty = 3)
legend("topleft", bty = "n", pch = c(16, 1, 4), cex = 0.9, legend = c("treated vs never treated", "earlier treated vs later control", "later treated vs earlier control"))
```

- 7a used the 2006 cohort against the never-treated. Now all $21$ adopting states, $2005$--$2009$, plus $29$ never adopters.
- TWFE: $\hat\delta = `r f3(coef(tw_cst))`$ ($`r f3(se(tw_cst))`$). The dotted line marks it.

## Castle doctrine: what is inside $`r f3(coef(tw_cst))`$

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
 & Weight & Average $2 \times 2$ \\
\midrule
Treated vs never treated & $`r f2(bcs$weight[3])`$ & $`r f3(bcs$avg[3])`$ \\
Earlier treated vs later control & $`r f2(bcs$weight[1])`$ & $`r f3(bcs$avg[1])`$ \\
Later treated vs earlier control (forbidden) & $`r f2(bcs$weight[2])`$ & $`r f3(bcs$avg[2])`$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

- $`r nrow(bc)`$ simple $2 \times 2$'s. The 2006-vs-never cell alone carries weight $`r f2(bc$w[bc$type == "Treated vs never treated" & bc$k == 2006])`$.
- With a large never-treated group, the forbidden comparisons get little weight and TWFE is close to the clean answer.
- That is **luck of the design**, not a property of the estimator. Check it every time.

## Conclusion

1. **Sampling can break parallel trends** with no change in behaviour: attrition that depends on $Y^0$, or a repeated cross-section whose composition shifts at treatment.
2. **Triple differences** assumes equal bias in two DiDs, not zero bias in one.
3. **Covariates** make parallel trends conditional. IPW, outcome regression and doubly robust estimators use it properly; TWFE with additive controls also assumes homogeneous effects and constant covariate returns.
4. **Under differential timing, TWFE averages every $2 \times 2$**, weighted by group size and treatment variance, including comparisons whose control was already treated.
5. With **dynamic effects** it can get the sign wrong while every textbook assumption holds.

\vspace{0.4em}

- **Next (7c):** estimators that never use an already-treated control, and how to read their event studies.

# Backup

## Stata: the estimators of this lecture

```stata
* covariates: IPW, outcome regression, doubly robust (two periods)
drdid y x1 x2, time(year) ivar(id) tr(treat) all     // reports ipw, reg, dripw, ...
teffects ipw (dy) (treat x1 x2), atet                 // IPW on the long difference

* differential timing: TWFE and its decomposition
use https://raw.githubusercontent.com/scunning1975/mixtape/master/baker.dta, clear
areg y i.year treat, a(id) robust                     // TWFE static = -6.69
bacondecomp y treat, ddetail                          // Goodman-Bacon weights and 2x2s
```

- R equivalents: `DRDID` (`drdid`), `bacondecomp`. This deck computes the Bacon decomposition from group means with base R and `fixest` only.
